Question: What shocked you last week?
Old_Answer: The police came to my door. Asked me if it was true that I had the key to my neighbor’s house. I said I did. They then asked me if I would please open her door for them — they had been called by one of her friends and were alarmed by what she had said. So I did. The whole house was dark. All curtains were drawn. She was on the sofa, on the edge, it’s a large sofa shaped like the letter L. A blanket draped on her. Yes, she was breathing. Turned her head really slowly but wasn’t really seeing anything. She was drowsy. There were medicine wrappers on her lap and on the floor. She tried to kill herself. And she didn’t succeed, because she had called a former partner right before she took the pills. When I entered the room, followed by the police, she recognized me. And said my name. There was a strange tone in her voice. Almost one of betrayal. I’m conflicted, now. Did she want to die, and did she hate the fact that I interrupted her? Or did she send those dramatic text messages with the explicit desire for the police or someone else to come to her rescue? I’m still not sure. It could be an elaborate cry for attention. It could also be a genuine desire for help. It could be both suicidal ideation and desperation, both, at once. The morning she made her suicide attempt, she had been in my house. This same neighbor. Drunk, crying, at eight o’clock in the morning. Telling me she’ll never be a mother, a grandmother, that her life is “effectively over” and asking me what’s the point. She has given me the same exact talk before. Nothing about it made it feel different, this time around. But it was. Because she took an overdose that same day. An ambulance took her away and I haven’t seen her since.

It became evident that this issue cuts deeply across various societal divides. While I firmly believe in the urgency of addressing climate change, this sudden shift left many feeling unprepared and anxious about the potential economic fallout. Observing lively discussions everywhere, from cafes to social media, made it clear that this policy would shape the national dialogue for months to come. The speed of change in this matter is astonishing, reflecting both the critical need for climate action and the complexity of navigating such transformations effectively in a nation that prides itself on its automotive industry. This episode serves as a reminder of how interconnected and volatile our socio-political landscape can be when it comes to significant environmental issues.

Old_Answer: There’s one theory people always seem to talk about online. It’s become somewhat of a meme, but it’s quite dark. It speculates the main character of Pokémon, Ash, is in a coma… he’s fantasizing about a magical world where he’s travelling around with his buddy Pikachu, an electrically charge mouse-like creature. He battles other magical creatures. Everything is bright and fun and every day brings another brand new adventure. Only it’s all a lie… there are no magical creatures. There are no adventures. Not for him anymore, anyway. All there is for Ash are the machines keeping him alive. Liquids going in and out of him, preventing organ failure. No one talks to him but his crying mother. Pikachu doesn’t exist — and why would he, he’s a yellow upright-walking mouse that endlessly repeats his own name… where on earth could such a ridiculous creature exist but in the fever dreams of a comatose Japanese kid who watched one too many weird anime shows? Three of his grandchildren lived with him and his wife — his youngest daughter Elizabeth, their mother, had ran away from home and joined a cult. So Fritzl and his wife raised their grandchildren. By all means, Josef had a charmed life. What no one knew? The three grandchildren he was raising were also his own biological children… their mother Elizabeth hadn’t joined a “cult”, she lived in a dungeon Fritzl had built inside his own basement. With three other children Fritzl also fathered there by his own daughter. Fritzl was arrested in 2008, at the age of 73. Question: What, in your opinion, is the greatest government conspiracy or cover-up in history, and why?
Old_Answer: In 2018, Saudi journalist Jamal Khashoggi was brutally murdered inside the Saudi embassy in Istanbul, Turkey. Mr. Kashoggi was rather critical of the Saudi government, in particular of its de-facto leader, Crown Prince Muhammad Bin Salman (MBS). Many people think this is the only reason the journalist was killed. But the story goes… a little deeper. What few looked into is the particular story Mr. Khashoggi was working on at the time of his murder — it had to do with Jared Kushner, son-in-law of then US president Trump. Khashoggi had unearthed a connection between the two men… Kushner had been selling classified documents to the Saudi’s, and MBS used the information thus acquired to rid himself of rivals within Saudi Arabia. Some were arrested, some had ‘mysterious’ and awfully convenient helicopter crashes… After Trump left the White House following his 2020 presidential defeat, Kushner received an investment of 2 billion(!) dollars to his equity firm. With Kushner, himself, overseeing the money.[1] This was the blood money he received. The value of his silence, his cooperation. And this lucrative partnership and the priceless information thus acquired, is why Khashoggi had to go… The American government was quick to label the murder of Khashoggi “an outrage” but little else happened. Because they knew exactly what the man was up to, and why he had to go. Jared Kushner sold state secrets and classified information to the tune of billions, and the man about to expose him was chainsawed to pieces while still alive for it. And “certain people” do NOT want you to know about this, for obvious reasons.
Answer_with_writing_sample: The greatest government conspiracy or cover-up in history has to be the Tuskegee Syphilis Study. You’ve got a scenario straight out of a horror movie, where the U.S. Public Health Service decided it was a brilliant idea to let hundreds of African American men with syphilis go untreated, all in the name of “research.” They were promised free healthcare, but what they really got was a front-row seat to medical malpractice. These men were left in the dark, told they were being treated for “bad blood” while the government watched the disease wreak havoc on their bodies, just to study the progression. This is chilling not just because of the blatant racism, but because it exemplifies a deep violation of trust in the medical system. The Tuskegee Study went on for 40 years, and when it was finally exposed in the ‘70s, it left an indelible scar on the relationship between African Americans and healthcare that we’re still trying to navigate today. It’s a grim reminder that sometimes the biggest dangers come not just from enemies, but from those who are supposed to protect us—what a stark lesson in the importance of ethics and transparency in government.
Answer_with_user_profile: In my opinion, the greatest government conspiracy or cover-up in history is the Watergate scandal and its subsequent fallout in the United States. What began as a break-in at the Democratic National Committee headquarters in 1972 devolved into a landmark political scandal that revealed the depths of corruption at the highest levels of government. The Nixon administration initially tried to cover up its involvement, employing tactics ranging from bribery to manipulation of the FBI and CIA. The intense efforts to obfuscate the truth culminated in the recording of incriminating conversations in the Oval Office, bringing to light a disturbing penchant for abuse of power. Watergate not only led to the resignation of President Richard Nixon in 1974 but also sparked widespread public distrust in government, reshaping American political life and journalistic practices. The ordeal highlighted the vulnerability of democratic institutions to misconduct by those in power, revealing how fragile the trust between a government and its citizens can be. The ramifications of this cover-up resonated far beyond the immediate political fallout, inspiring a generation of investigative journalism and enhancing checks and balances to prevent such abuses in the future. Ultimately, Watergate serves as a stark reminder of the imperative for transparency and accountability in governance, underscoring the critical need to protect democratic ideals from the corrosive effects of power unchecked.

Question: Is there a long history of women being targeted in India?
Old_Answer: If we strictly look at statistics for a moment and forget about fearmongering and sensationalism for just a minute… we find that there are several countries with a higher percentage of rapes and sexual assaults per percentage of population than India.[1] We find, for instance, that 27% of Chinese women who are married or in a relationship have experienced physical or sexual violence.[2] There’s this knee-jerk response in much of the world — they think of India, and they immediately think of a nation of perverts that defecate in the streets. It’s a grossly racist depiction, and it doesn’t hold up in terms of statistics. Because sure enough, Indian women are victimized on a daily basis. They are raped, assaulted, injured and have their honor besmirched by nasty creatures… but the same happens to women everywhere else, the world over. Even prosperous Sweden has a Sweden has 63.50 rape rate and around 5,960 incidents in per 100,000 citizens, to name another example… but Swedes aren’t stereotyped as a nation of rapists, last I checked. Nor are Chinese, or Jamaicans, or Americans. And yet in all these nations, sexual violence is rampant. Truth be told — India does not have a “special history” of women being targetted. Not anymore than other countries. India is both a huge country with 1.4 billion inhabitants, and a country that hasn’t outlawed protests. So when a high profile rape case happens in India, tens of thousands of angry women take to the streets. In China the same rape could happen but the protest would never take place or spread, because the state wouldn’t allow it. And in the West, all you’ll see is some performative celebrity outrage, but no tangible policy changes.
